references.text: Jesus uses the same image of salt that loses its flavor in the Sermon on the Mount: it is good for nothing, but is thrown out and trampled underfoot by people ([ref:Matt 5:13|Matthew 5:13]).
Mark's parallel about salt that loses its savor and cannot be made salty again ([ref:Mark 9:50|Mark 9:50]).
The same phrasing, "He who has ears to hear, let him hear!" is used by Jesus also in [ref:Matt 11:15|Matthew 11:15], as an encouragement for spiritual attentiveness.
Jesus concludes the parable of the sower with the same expression: "He who has ears, let him hear!" ([ref:Matt 13:9|Matthew 13:9]).
In Revelation, the call is repeated, "He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches" ([ref:Rev 2:7|Revelation 2:7]), as an echo of Jesus' words.
Also in Mark, Jesus uses the phrasing, "He who has ears to hear, let him hear!" ([ref:Mark 4:9|Mark 4:9]).
Earlier in Luke's Gospel, Jesus uses the same expression, "He who has ears to hear, let him hear!" after the parable of the sower ([ref:Luke 8:8|Luke 8:8]).
Ezekiel uses the image of something useless being thrown into the fire, in a similar way as the worthless salt is cast out ([ref:Ezek 15:5|Ezekiel 15:5]).
The image in Hebrews of land that bears thorns and thistles and is near to being cursed is a related picture of what is useless and rejected ([ref:Heb 6:7-8|Hebrews 6:7-8]).
